decks.title: Staffing — Part 1: Meaning, Process and Recruitment
goals: Explain the meaning and importance of staffing and its place in human resource management
Describe the steps of the staffing process, including workload and workforce analysis
Compare internal and external sources of recruitment and choose a suitable source for a job

slides.heading: Staffing
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what staffing is, why it matters, the **staffing process** and **recruitment**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what staffing is, why it matters, staffing and human resource management, the staffing process, and recruitment from internal and external sources
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every organisation, from a corner bakery to a large hospital, depends on people. Machines and money are useless without the right people to use them. In this chapter we study staffing, the function of management that finds, chooses, trains and keeps the right people. Part 1 covers what staffing is, why it matters, its eight steps, and where firms look for new employees.

slides.heading: What is staffing?
slides.body_md: **Staffing** means filling, and keeping filled, the positions in the organisation structure with **suitable people**.
bullets: Organising creates posts; staffing puts people into them.
It is a continuous function: people retire, resign and are promoted.
It is performed by **every manager**, not only by a human resource department.

rows: How to guide and motivate them?

visual.alt: Table placing staffing among the functions of management: planning asks what to do, organising creates jobs, staffing asks who will do each job, directing guides people and controlling checks progress
visual.caption: Organising creates posts; staffing fills them.

slides.narration: Organising divides work into jobs and posts. Staffing answers the next question: who will do each job? Because people keep retiring, resigning and moving up, staffing never stops. And it is not only the job of a human resource department; every manager chooses, trains and appraises the people working under him or her.

slides.heading: Why staffing matters

rows: Capable candidates are found for every post
Ability matches the job, so output rises
Successors are ready when seniors leave
Neither idle workers nor endless overtime
Fair hiring, training and pay keep people satisfied

visual.alt: Table of five benefits of good staffing: competent people, the right person on the right job, continuity through successors, optimum use of people, and better morale

slides.narration: Good staffing brings five benefits. It finds competent people. It puts the right person on the right job, so performance improves. It prepares successors, so the business keeps running when senior people leave. It avoids both idle workers and endless overtime. And fair hiring, training and pay keep people satisfied, which lowers absenteeism and turnover.

slides.heading: Quick check: the meaning of staffing
slides.body_md: Which description fits staffing as a function of management?
slides.narration: Think about which function deals with people for the posts that already exist. Rule out dividing work, guiding people, and checking performance.

slides.heading: Staffing and human resource management
slides.body_md: Managing people at work has widened over time. Staffing is a **part** of human resource management (HRM).

nodes.label: Human resource management (people as a resource to develop)

visual.alt: Flow of how managing people at work has widened: from a labour welfare officer, to personnel management, to human resource management
visual.caption: Managing people: a widening role

slides.narration: In early factories, a labour welfare officer looked after workers. Later, personnel departments kept records, paid wages and enforced rules. Today firms speak of human resource management, which treats people as a resource to be developed. Staffing, that is recruiting, selecting, training and paying people, sits at the heart of human resource management.

slides.heading: Specialised activities of HRM

rows: Studying what a lab-technician job needs and finding applicants
Running a safety course for new workers
Defending the firm in labour cases

visual.alt: Table of specialised human resource activities with examples: recruitment and job analysis, compensation plans, training, employee and union relations, welfare and social security, and legal matters

slides.narration: In a large firm, a human resource department handles specialised work: studying jobs and finding applicants, designing pay and incentives, running training, meeting unions and handling grievances, providing welfare such as health cover and provident fund, and defending the firm in labour cases. Notice that pricing or advertising products is not on this list; those belong to marketing.

visual.caption: The staffing process: it starts with estimating manpower needs.

slides.narration: Staffing follows eight steps. First estimate how many people are needed. Then recruit, which means attracting applicants, and select the best. Place them in their jobs and introduce them to the organisation. Train and develop them. Appraise their performance, promote deserving people and plan their careers, and finally decide their compensation. Learn this order; it is often asked.

slides.heading: Step 1: estimating manpower requirements
slides.body_md: Two analyses are compared:

rows: How many people, and of what kind, are **needed**?
How many people, and of what kind, are **available**?

visual.alt: Table comparing workload analysis, which finds the people needed from planned output, with workforce analysis, which finds the people available from present staff; comparing them gives the shortage or surplus
visual.caption: Needed minus available = shortage (recruit) or surplus (redeploy).

slides.narration: The first step needs two studies. Workload analysis asks how many people, and of what kind, are needed for the planned work. Workforce analysis asks how many people, and of what kind, the firm already has, allowing for retirements and resignations. Subtract available from needed. A positive gap means recruit; a negative gap means a surplus to transfer or retrain.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many to recruit?
slides.body_md: An imagined bakery must bake 7,200 loaves a day; one baker bakes 360. It has 16 bakers, and 1 will retire.
bullets: Step 1 — Workload: 7,200 ÷ 360 = **20 bakers needed**.
Step 2 — Workforce: 16 − 1 = **15 available**.
Step 3 — Shortage: 20 − 15 = **5 to recruit**.

slides.narration: Let us estimate for an imagined bakery. It must bake seven thousand two hundred loaves a day, and one baker bakes three hundred and sixty. Dividing gives twenty bakers needed. It has sixteen bakers, but one will retire, so fifteen are available. Twenty minus fifteen gives five bakers to recruit. Always allow for people who are leaving.

slides.heading: Quick check: the order of staffing
slides.body_md: Arrange five steps of the staffing process in order.
slides.narration: Start with knowing the need. Then think: attract applicants, choose, place, and finally train.

slides.heading: Steps 4 to 8

rows: Newcomer takes up the post and is introduced to people, place and rules
Skills for the present job; growth for future roles
Actual performance compared with standards; feedback given
Higher posts for deserving staff; a path for growth
Direct pay (salary, incentives) and indirect benefits (insurance, paid leave)

visual.alt: Table of the later staffing steps: placement and orientation, training and development, performance appraisal, promotion and career planning, and compensation in direct and indirect forms

slides.narration: After selection, the new employee is placed in the post and introduced to colleagues, the workplace and its rules; this is orientation. Training builds job skills, and development prepares the person for the future. Performance appraisal compares actual work with standards. Deserving people are promoted and their careers planned. Compensation covers direct pay such as salary and incentives, and indirect benefits such as insurance and paid leave.

slides.body_md: Fill in the blank about the study of employees already available.
slides.narration: Is the manager looking at work to be done, or at the people already on the rolls?

slides.heading: Recruitment
slides.body_md: **Recruitment** is searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. It is a **positive** process: it widens the pool.

visual.alt: Flow of recruitment: a vacancy is identified, sources are searched, job seekers are encouraged to apply, and a pool of applicants is formed for selection
visual.caption: Recruitment builds the pool

slides.narration: Recruitment is the search for prospective employees and the effort to make them apply. Its aim is a large pool of suitable applicants, which is why it is called a positive process. Firms can look inside the organisation, through transfers and promotions, or outside, through many external sources.

slides.heading: Internal sources: transfer and promotion

rows: Sideways: another job, department or place
Fill a gap, reduce surplus elsewhere, broaden experience
Reward and motivate; fill senior posts

visual.alt: Table comparing transfer, a sideways move with no substantial change in pay, and promotion, an upward move to a higher post with more pay and status

slides.narration: There are two internal sources. A transfer moves an employee sideways, to another job, department or place, with no big change in pay or status. It fills gaps and reduces surpluses elsewhere. A promotion moves an employee up to a higher post with more pay, responsibility and status. It rewards good work and motivates others.

slides.heading: Internal sources: merits and limitations
columns:
**Merits**
- Employees are motivated
- Candidates are known
- Surplus and shortage adjusted
- Cheaper

**Limitations**
- No fresh talent
- Complacency
- Not for a new firm
- Frequent transfers disrupt work

rows: No fresh talent or new ideas
Candidates already known, so selection is simpler
Transfers can adjust surplus and shortage
A new firm cannot use them

visual.alt: Table of merits of internal sources (motivation, known candidates, adjusting staff, low cost) and limitations (no fresh talent, complacency, unusable by a new firm, disruption from frequent transfers)

slides.narration: Internal sources motivate employees, make selection simpler because the firm knows its own people, adjust staff between units, and cost little. But they shut out new ideas, may make staff complacent if they expect promotion by seniority, cannot be used by a new firm that has no staff yet, and frequent transfers can lower productivity.

slides.heading: External sources of recruitment

rows: Notice at the premises; walk-in hiring
Any job, when a vacancy arises
Search and screen for a fee
Many jobs; candidates are vouched for

visual.alt: Table of nine external sources of recruitment with how each works and the jobs it suits, from direct recruitment and casual callers to placement agencies, campus recruitment, labour contractors and web publishing

slides.narration: Firms have many external sources. A notice at the gate, called direct recruitment, suits casual and unskilled jobs. Casual callers leave applications on file. Advertisements reach a wide audience. Employment exchanges keep a government register of job seekers. Placement agencies and consultants find senior and technical people for a fee. Firms also visit campuses, accept employees' recommendations, use labour contractors and publish vacancies on the web.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: matching sources to jobs
slides.body_md: An imagined hospital in Pune has four vacancies. Choose a source for each.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: what level and skill does the job need?
Step 2 — Ask: how urgent is it?
Step 3 — Ask: is there a capable insider?
Step 4 — Name the source and give the reason.

headers: Vacancy at an imagined Pune hospital
rows: A head of the billing unit
A capable senior clerk is already there

visual.alt: Worked example table matching four imagined hospital vacancies to sources: ward helpers through a contractor or direct recruitment, nurses through campus recruitment, a cardiologist through a placement consultant, and a billing head by promotion
visual.caption: Match the source to the level, skill and urgency of the job.

slides.narration: Here is how to choose. Twenty ward helpers needed this week are unskilled and urgent, so use a labour contractor or direct recruitment. Ten fresh nurses can come from campus recruitment. A chief cardiologist is rare and senior, so hire a placement consultant. For the head of billing, a capable senior clerk already exists, so promote from within.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the source
slides.body_md: Job seekers leave applications at a hotel even without a vacancy. Which source is this?
slides.narration: The applications were not invited for any particular vacancy. What do we call such applicants?

slides.heading: External sources: merits and limitations
columns:
**Merits**
- Qualified personnel
- Wider choice
- Fresh talent
- Competitive spirit

**Limitations**
- Staff dissatisfaction
- Lengthy
- Costly
- Uncertain response

visual.alt: Table of merits of external sources (qualified people, wider choice, fresh talent, competition) and limitations (staff dissatisfaction, a lengthy process, cost, uncertain response)

slides.narration: External sources bring qualified people, a wider choice and fresh ideas, and they keep insiders alert. But existing employees who hoped for promotion may feel let down. The process is lengthy and costly, with advertisements, fees and tests, and the response is not always good. Most firms therefore use a mix of internal and external sources.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

nodes.label: Staffing fills posts with suitable people
Part of HRM; every manager's job
Process: estimate needs → recruit → select → place → train → appraise → promote → pay
Recruitment: internal (transfer, promotion) or external (nine sources)

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: staffing fills posts; it is part of human resource management and every manager's job; the eight-step process; and internal and external recruitment
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Staffing fills posts with suitable people and is every manager's job, as well as a part of human resource management. The process has eight steps, starting with workload and workforce analysis. Recruitment searches for applicants, inside the firm through transfers and promotions, or outside through nine sources, each with its merits and limits.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Workload = people **needed**; workforce = people **available**. Do not swap them.
Transfer is **sideways**; promotion is **upwards** with more pay and status.
In case questions, **quote the line** and then name the source or step.
A new business **cannot** use internal sources.
3-mark answers: three points with a line each (about 50–80 words); 5-mark answers: five points.
slides.narration: Some tips for the exam. Keep workload and workforce analysis apart: needed versus available. A transfer is a sideways move, a promotion an upward one. In case-based questions, first quote the exact line and then name the source or step; both earn marks. Remember that a brand-new business cannot recruit internally. Write one point per mark, each explained in a line.

decks.title: Staffing — Part 2: Selection, Training and Development
goals: Explain the steps of the selection process and the purpose of each selection test
Distinguish training, development and education, and state the benefits of training
Choose suitable on-the-job and off-the-job training methods for given situations

slides.heading: Selection, training and development
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how firms **choose** the best applicants and **develop** them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: meaning of selection, selection tests, the later steps of selection, training versus development, and training methods
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Recruitment gave us a pool of applicants. Now the firm must choose the best of them and then help them grow. In Part 2 we study the steps of selection, the five selection tests, the difference between training and development, and the methods firms use to train people on the job and off the job.

slides.heading: What is selection?
slides.body_md: **Selection** is identifying and choosing the best persons from among the prospective candidates for a job.

visual.alt: Table comparing recruitment, a positive process that attracts applicants and comes first, with selection, a negative process that rejects applicants until the best remain

slides.narration: Selection means identifying and choosing the best candidates from the pool. Recruitment is called positive because it invites people to apply. Selection is called negative because, at every step, some applicants are rejected, until only the most suitable remain. Selection always follows recruitment.

slides.heading: The selection process

visual.alt: Flow of the eight steps of selection: preliminary screening, selection tests, employment interview, reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer, and contract of employment
visual.caption: Selection, step by step

slides.narration: Selection has eight steps. Preliminary screening removes clearly unsuitable applicants. Selection tests measure ability. An interview judges suitability in depth. References and background are checked. Then the selection decision is made. A medical examination follows, then the job offer, and finally both sides sign the contract of employment.

slides.heading: Screening and selection tests
slides.body_md: **Preliminary screening** uses the application form to drop unqualified applicants. Then **tests** measure ability:

rows: How would you handle an angry customer?
Wire a switchboard; type a letter
Would you rather fix machines or meet clients?

visual.alt: Table of five selection tests: intelligence measures general mental ability, aptitude measures potential to learn, personality measures emotions and values, trade measures existing skill, and interest measures likes and dislikes about work

slides.narration: Screening uses the application form to drop those without the minimum qualification. Then come tests. An intelligence test measures general mental ability. An aptitude test measures the potential to learn new skills. A personality test looks at emotions, maturity and values. A trade test measures the skill a person already has. An interest test finds what kind of work the person likes.

slides.heading: Quick check: which test?
slides.body_md: Trainee pilots are tested on how quickly they can learn new coordination skills. Which test is this?
slides.narration: The candidates have no flying skill yet. Is the test about present skill or about potential to learn?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the right test
slides.body_md: Pick the most useful test for four imagined vacancies.
bullets: Step 1 — Does the candidate already have the skill? If not, test **aptitude**.
Step 2 — If the skill is claimed, test it with a **trade** test.
Step 3 — If dealing with people and stress matters, use a **personality** test.
Step 4 — For general reasoning, use an **intelligence** test.

visual.alt: Worked example table choosing a test for four imagined vacancies: aptitude for a trainee crane operator, trade for an experienced typist, personality for a customer-care executive and intelligence for a management trainee
visual.caption: Potential to learn → aptitude; present skill → trade.

slides.narration: Let us choose tests. A trainee crane operator has no experience, so we ask whether he can learn: an aptitude test. An experienced typist claims a skill, so we check it with a trade test. A customer-care executive must stay calm with angry callers: a personality test. A management trainee needs sharp reasoning: an intelligence test.

slides.heading: From interview to contract

rows: In-depth conversation: judge suitability, share information
Verify record and character with referees and past employers
Final choice, usually by the manager concerned
Signed terms: duties, pay, hours, leave, termination

visual.alt: Table of the later steps of selection and their purpose: interview, reference checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer, and contract of employment

slides.narration: The interview is a detailed, two-way conversation: the firm judges the candidate and also gives information about the job. Reference checks verify the candidate's record and character. The manager concerned then makes the selection decision. A medical examination checks fitness. The job offer is an appointment letter with a joining date, and the signed contract sets out duties, pay, hours, leave and terms of termination.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of selection
slides.body_md: Arrange six steps of selection in order.
slides.narration: Begin with the step that uses the application form, and end with the step that checks physical fitness.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a case
slides.body_md: Identify the step of selection from lines in an imagined case about Pragati Textiles.
bullets: Step 1 — Read each line slowly.
Step 2 — Look for the key action: setting aside, testing, phoning, examining.
Step 3 — Name the step and quote the line.

headers: Line from an imagined case (Pragati Textiles)
rows: "Applicants without a textile diploma were set aside."

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and importance of staffing
sections.body_md:
Staffing is the managerial function of **filling, and keeping filled, the posts** created by organising with suitable people. It is **continuous** (people retire, resign, move up) and is done by **every manager**.

**Importance**
1. Finds **competent personnel** for all jobs.
2. Puts the **right person on the right job**, improving performance.
3. Ensures **continuity and growth** through succession planning.
4. Ensures **optimum use** of people, avoiding over-manning and under-manning.
5. Raises **job satisfaction and morale** through fair hiring, training and pay.

key_terms.definition_md: Filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure with suitable people.

Fewer employees than the work needs, which causes delays and overtime.

sections.heading: 2. Staffing as a part of human resource management
sections.body_md:
The management of people widened from a **labour welfare officer**, to **personnel management**, to **human resource management**, which treats people as a resource to develop. Staffing is a part of HRM.

**Specialised HRM activities:** recruitment and job analysis; compensation and incentive plans; training and development; union–management relations and grievance handling; welfare and social security; defending the firm in labour cases.

sections.heading: 4. Recruitment and its sources
sections.body_md:
**Recruitment:** searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply (a **positive** process).

**Internal sources**
- **Transfer:** sideways move, no substantial change in pay or status.
- **Promotion:** upward move with more pay, responsibility and status.

Merits: motivation, known candidates, adjusting staff, low cost. Limitations: no fresh talent, complacency, not usable by a new firm, disruption from frequent transfers.

**External sources:** direct recruitment, casual callers, advertisement, employment exchange, placement agencies and management consultants, campus recruitment, recommendations of employees, labour contractors, web publishing.

Merits: qualified people, wider choice, fresh talent, competition. Limitations: staff dissatisfaction, lengthy, costly, uncertain response.

sections.body_md:
**Selection:** identifying and choosing the best candidates from the pool (a **negative** process, since it rejects).

1. **Preliminary screening** (application forms).
2. **Selection tests:** intelligence (IQ), aptitude (potential to learn), personality (emotions, maturity, values), trade (existing skill), interest (likes and dislikes).
3. **Employment interview:** in-depth, two-way conversation.
4. **Reference and background checks**.
5. **Selection decision** (by the manager concerned).
6. **Medical examination**.
7. **Job offer** (appointment letter).
8. **Contract of employment** (job title, duties, pay, hours, leave, termination).

questions.stem_md: Staffing, as a function of management, is best described as

options.text_md: dividing the work of an enterprise into departments and jobs
filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure with suitable people
guiding, instructing and motivating people at work
comparing actual performance with the standards set in advance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure with suitable people. Staffing is about people: finding, placing, developing and keeping the right people in the positions that organising has created. Dividing work is organising, guiding people is directing, and comparing performance with standards is controlling.

questions.stem_md: Rangoli Prints (imagined), a textile unit in Surat, found that some departments had idle workers while others were working overtime. Better staffing would mainly help it by

options.text_md: removing the need for any supervision of workers
guaranteeing that the firm earns a profit every year
replacing the planning function of management
ensuring optimum use of human resources by avoiding both over-manning and under-manning

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ensuring optimum use of human resources by avoiding both over-manning and under-manning. Matching the number and kind of workers to the work avoids over-manning (idle staff) and under-manning (overtime, delays). Staffing does not remove supervision, cannot guarantee profit and does not replace planning.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is **NOT** a specialised activity of a human resource department?

options.text_md: Fixing the selling price of the firm's products
Handling grievances and complaints of employees
Maintaining relations between management and unions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Fixing the selling price of the firm's products. Pricing is a marketing decision. Compensation plans, grievance handling and union–management relations are all part of human resource management.

questions.stem_md: Which sequence shows how the management of people at work has broadened over time?

options.text_md: Human resource management → personnel management → labour welfare officer
Personnel management → labour welfare officer → human resource management
Labour welfare officer → personnel management → human resource management
Labour welfare officer → human resource management → personnel management

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Labour welfare officer → personnel management → human resource management. Firms first appointed a welfare officer to look after workers, then built personnel departments, and today treat people as a resource to be developed through human resource management.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Staffing is often called an integral part of human resource management.

**Reason (R):** Human resource management covers recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and paying people, which are the very activities of staffing.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the activities that make up staffing are the core of human resource management, so staffing is one of its parts.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Staffing is the duty of every manager and not only of the human resource department.

**Reason (R):** In large organisations a separate human resource department is set up to handle specialised staffing activities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because every manager chooses, trains and appraises the people under them. R is a separate fact about how big firms organise specialised work.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A tailoring shop in Ludhiana (imagined) with six workers does not perform the staffing function, because it has no human resource department.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Even a small firm must find, choose, train and pay its workers; the owner simply performs the staffing function personally. A separate department is needed only when a firm grows large.

questions.stem_md: Give any two reasons why staffing is important for an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: competent people, right person on the right job, succession and continuity, optimum use of people, job satisfaction and morale.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Competent personnel:** staffing helps discover and obtain **capable people** for different jobs.
2. **Continuity and growth:** by developing managers through **succession planning**, it keeps the business running smoothly even when senior people leave or retire.

questions.stem_md: Human resource management is a wider concept than staffing. State any three specialised activities that a human resource department performs.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct specialised activities, each with a short explanation.

questions.stem_md: Explain the importance of staffing for an organisation, giving five points.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct points, each with a heading and one line of explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Obtaining competent personnel:** staffing helps the firm discover and attract **capable people** for its jobs.
2. **Right person on the right job:** matching ability to the job raises **performance and output**.
3. **Survival and growth:** **succession planning** prepares people to take over senior posts, so the business continues smoothly.
4. **Optimum use of people:** it avoids **over-manning** (idle workers, higher costs) and **under-manning** (overtime, delays).
5. **Job satisfaction:** fair selection, training and pay improve **morale** and reduce absenteeism and turnover.

questions.stem_md: The first step of the staffing process is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** estimating manpower requirements. A firm must first know how many people, and of what kind, it needs; only then can it search for and choose them.

questions.stem_md: The HR head of Kaveri Pumps (imagined), Coimbatore, studies how many machinists, fitters and inspectors are needed to produce next year's target output. This study is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** workload analysis. Working out the number and types of people **needed** for the planned work is workload analysis. Workforce analysis looks at the people **available**; appraisal rates past performance; job rotation is a training method.

questions.stem_md: Before hiring, the manager of Saffron Foods (imagined) lists the skills, ages and expected retirements of the 40 workers already on the rolls. She is doing
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** workforce analysis. Studying the number and kind of employees **already available** is workforce analysis. Comparing it with the workload shows the shortage or surplus.

questions.stem_md: On her first day at Meghdoot Couriers (imagined), Ritika is shown around the office, introduced to her team and told the leave rules. This step of staffing is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** orientation. Introducing a new employee to the people, place and rules of the organisation is orientation (induction). It follows selection and comes with placement.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an **indirect** financial payment to an employee?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Paid vacation and health insurance. Indirect payments are benefits such as paid leave and insurance. Salary, commission and piece wages are direct payments for work done.

questions.stem_md: Tejas Electronics (imagined) tells every new engineer which higher posts they can reach in five years and what skills each post needs. This reflects which step of staffing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Promotion and career planning. Showing employees the path to higher posts and what they need to reach them is career planning, which goes with promotion. It keeps capable people motivated to stay.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps of the staffing process in the correct order.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (a) → (e) → (c) → (b). Need is estimated first, candidates are attracted, the best are chosen, they are placed and introduced, and then they are trained and developed.

questions.stem_md: Studying the number and type of employees already available in the organisation is called ___ analysis.
questions.solution_md: This is workforce analysis; workload analysis finds the number and type of people needed.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pickle unit in Jaipur must pack 12,600 jars a month. One packer can pack 450 jars a month, and the unit has 22 packers now. How many more packers must it recruit?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 (workload analysis): packers needed = 12,600 ÷ 450 = 28.
Step 2 (workforce analysis): packers available = 22.
Step 3: shortage = 28 − 22 = 6 packers to recruit.

questions.stem_md: An imagined call centre in Mohali expects 9,000 customer calls a week. Each agent can handle 300 calls a week. It has 27 agents, but 3 of them will retire this month. How many agents must it recruit to meet the workload?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 (workload): agents needed = 9,000 ÷ 300 = 30.
Step 2 (workforce): agents available = 27 − 3 = 24.
Step 3: agents to recruit = 30 − 24 = 6.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because appraisal reveals where an employee falls short or excels, it shows who needs training and who deserves promotion.

questions.stem_md: How do workload analysis and workforce analysis together help a manager estimate manpower requirements?
questions.solution_md: Define both analyses and state that their comparison gives the shortage or surplus.

answer.model_answer_md: **Workload analysis** finds the number and types of people **needed** to do the planned work. **Workforce analysis** finds the number and types **already available**. Comparing the two shows whether the firm has a **shortage** to recruit for or a **surplus** to redeploy.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between placement and orientation of a newly selected employee.
questions.solution_md: One clear sentence on each term.

answer.model_answer_md: **Placement** means the employee **occupying the position** or post for which they were selected. **Orientation** (induction) means **introducing** the new employee to colleagues, superiors, the workplace and the **rules and policies** of the organisation.

questions.stem_md: Explain the last three steps of the staffing process that come after training and development.
questions.solution_md: Name the three steps in order and explain each in one or two lines.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Performance appraisal:** evaluating an employee's actual performance against the **standards** expected for the job, and giving feedback.
2. **Promotion and career planning:** moving deserving employees to **higher posts** with more responsibility, pay and status, and showing them a career path.
3. **Compensation:** fixing **pay and benefits**: direct payments such as salary and incentives, and indirect ones such as insurance and paid leave.

questions.stem_md: Explain the first five steps of the staffing process.
questions.solution_md: Five steps in the correct order, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Estimating manpower requirements:** **workload analysis** (people needed) and **workforce analysis** (people available) show the shortage or surplus.
2. **Recruitment:** **searching** for prospective employees and **stimulating** them to apply.
3. **Selection:** choosing the **most suitable** candidates from the pool through tests and interviews.
4. **Placement and orientation:** the selected person **takes up the post** and is **introduced** to colleagues, workplace and rules.
5. **Training and development:** improving the employee's **skills and knowledge** for the present job and for future growth.

questions.stem_md: Recruitment means

options.text_md: choosing the best candidate from those who have applied
improving the skills of employees for their present jobs
searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs
introducing a new employee to the workplace and colleagues

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs. Recruitment builds a pool of applicants. Choosing among them is selection, improving skills is training, and introducing a newcomer is orientation.

questions.stem_md: A branch manager of Godavari Cooperative Bank (imagined) is moved from Nashik to Pune at the same grade and pay because the Pune branch is short of a manager. This is an example of

options.text_md: promotion, an internal source of recruitment
transfer, an internal source of recruitment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** transfer, an internal source of recruitment. Shifting an employee to another job or place at the **same level**, without a substantial change in pay or responsibility, is a transfer, an internal source. A promotion means a higher post; job rotation is done to train, not to fill a vacancy.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about promotion as a source of recruitment is correct?

options.text_md: It brings fresh talent and new ideas from outside the organisation
It shifts an employee to another job at the same level
It is the most suitable source for a business that has just started
It moves an employee to a higher post with more responsibility, pay and status, and motivates others

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It moves an employee to a higher post with more responsibility, pay and status, and motivates others. Promotion fills a higher post from inside and motivates employees. It cannot bring outside talent, it is not a same-level move (that is a transfer), and a new business has no staff to promote.

questions.stem_md: Many job seekers walk into the office of Indrayani Hotels (imagined) and leave their applications even when no vacancy is advertised. The hotel keeps these on file and contacts them when posts fall vacant. This source of recruitment is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** casual callers. Unsolicited applicants whose details are kept for future vacancies are casual callers. It saves the cost of advertising for each vacancy.

questions.stem_md: A construction firm in Bhopal (imagined) pins a notice at its site gate: "Wanted: 15 helpers. Report at 8 a.m. tomorrow." Helpers who turn up are hired the same day. This source is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** direct recruitment. A notice at the gate for unskilled jobs, with on-the-spot hiring, is direct recruitment. It is cheap and quick for casual or unskilled vacancies.

questions.stem_md: Nilachal Steel (imagined) needs a chief technology officer with rare expertise. It hires an outside firm that searches for, screens and short-lists suitable senior professionals for a fee. The source used is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** placement agencies and management consultants. For technical, professional and top-level posts, firms pay placement agencies and management consultants to find and screen candidates. Employment exchanges mainly serve unskilled and skilled operative jobs.

questions.stem_md: Labour contractors are a suitable external source mainly for
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** unskilled workers needed quickly. Contractors keep in close touch with labourers and can supply unskilled workers at short notice. Senior and professional posts use consultants or advertisements; graduates come through campus recruitment.

questions.stem_md: Which is a merit of **external** sources of recruitment?

options.text_md: They are always cheaper and quicker than internal sources
They improve the morale of existing employees waiting for promotion
They make the selection process simpler because candidates are already known
They give management a wider choice and bring fresh talent into the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They give management a wider choice and bring fresh talent into the firm. External sources widen the pool and bring new skills and ideas. They are usually costlier and slower, may disappoint staff hoping for promotion, and the candidates are not already known.

questions.stem_md: Which is a **limitation** of filling vacancies only through internal sources?

options.text_md: Employees may become complacent if they expect promotion by seniority, and no fresh talent enters
Existing employees lose motivation because outsiders get the better jobs
The cost of advertising and testing becomes very high
The firm cannot know the past performance of the candidates

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Employees may become complacent if they expect promotion by seniority, and no fresh talent enters. Relying only on insiders shuts out new ideas and can make staff lethargic. The other options describe limitations of external sources or are false for internal ones (insiders' records are known).

**Assertion (A):** A newly started enterprise cannot depend on internal sources of recruitment.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a new firm has no existing staff to transfer or promote, so it must recruit from outside.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: advertising, testing and interviewing outsiders takes money and time. R is false: hiring outsiders for senior posts can **lower** the morale of employees who hoped to be promoted.

questions.stem_md: State one merit and one limitation of internal sources of recruitment.
questions.solution_md: One genuine merit and one genuine limitation, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Merit:** promotions **motivate employees** to work better, and selection is simpler because the candidates' records are **already known**.
**Limitation:** **no fresh talent** or new ideas enter the firm, and staff may become **complacent** if they expect promotion by seniority.

questions.stem_md: Recruitment is called a positive process and selection a negative one. Explain why.
questions.solution_md: Link "positive" to attracting applicants and "negative" to rejecting them.

answer.model_answer_md: Recruitment is **positive** because it **encourages as many suitable people as possible to apply**, building a large pool. Selection is **negative** because it **rejects** most applicants at each step until only the most suitable remain.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three external sources of recruitment, saying for which kind of job each is suitable.
questions.solution_md: Any three external sources, each with a line on how it works and the jobs it suits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Advertisement** in newspapers, journals or online: reaches a **wide** audience; suitable for **middle and senior** posts.
2. **Placement agencies and management consultants:** search and screen candidates for a fee; suitable for **technical, professional and top** posts.
3. **Labour contractors:** keep in touch with workers and supply them quickly; suitable for **unskilled** jobs.

questions.stem_md: Kesari Motors (imagined) has decided to fill all its senior posts from outside. Explain three problems this policy may create.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations of external sources, applied to the firm's policy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Dissatisfaction among staff:** existing employees who hoped for promotion may feel ignored, lowering **morale** and loyalty.
2. **Lengthy process:** advertising, testing and interviewing outsiders takes **a long time**, so posts stay vacant.
3. **Costly:** advertisements, agency fees and tests make external recruitment **expensive**, and the response is often **uncertain**.

questions.stem_md: Sahyadri Agro (imagined) fills most vacancies by transfers and promotions. Explain the two internal sources and any three merits of this policy for the company.
questions.solution_md: Explain both sources, then three merits with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Transfer:** shifting an employee to another job, department or place at the **same level**, without a substantial change in pay or status.
2. **Promotion:** moving an employee to a **higher post** with more responsibility, pay and status.
3. **Motivation:** the chance of promotion encourages employees to **improve their performance**.
4. **Simpler selection:** candidates are **already known**, so their record and suitability can be judged more reliably and quickly.
5. **Adjusting staff and lower cost:** transfers move surplus workers to short-staffed units, and no advertising or agency costs arise.

questions.stem_md: A new solar-panel company in Gandhinagar (imagined) must hire 200 people, from engineers to helpers. Recommend suitable sources of recruitment and evaluate the merits and limitations of relying on external sources.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Suitable sources:** **campus recruitment** for young engineers, **advertisement or web publishing** for experienced staff, and **labour contractors or direct recruitment** for helpers.
2. **Merit, fresh talent:** outsiders bring new skills, which a new company needs.
3. **Merit, wider choice:** a large pool lets the firm pick the **best-qualified** people.
4. **Limitations:** external recruitment is **costly** and **time-consuming**, and the response may be uncertain.
5. **Judgement:** as a **new** firm has no staff to promote, external sources are **unavoidable**; once running, it can mix in promotions to keep staff motivated.

questions.stem_md: Selection is the process of

options.text_md: creating a pool of applicants for a vacancy
moving an employee to a higher post
identifying and choosing the best persons from among the prospective candidates for a job
evaluating the performance of an employee after a year

questions.stem_md: Out of 900 applications for clerks at Vindhya Gramin Bank (imagined), 600 are rejected because the applicants do not have the minimum qualification stated in the advertisement. This step is

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an aptitude test. An aptitude test measures a person's **potential to learn** new skills. A trade test measures skills a person **already has**; an interest test finds likes and dislikes; an intelligence test measures general mental ability (IQ).

questions.stem_md: An imagined furniture firm in Saharanpur asks applicants for carpenters to make a small drawer in two hours to check their existing woodworking skill. The test used is

emotions, reactions, maturity and value system

questions.stem_md: What is the purpose of the employment interview in the selection process?
questions.solution_md: Two purposes: assessing suitability and exchanging information.

answer.model_answer_md: The interview is an **in-depth conversation** with the candidate to judge **suitability** for the job. It also lets the firm **give information** about the job and organisation, and lets the candidate seek information.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three steps of selection that come after the selection decision.
questions.solution_md: Three steps in order, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Medical examination:** the selected candidate is checked for **physical fitness** for the job before the offer is made.
2. **Job offer:** a **letter of appointment** confirms the post and states the date by which the candidate must join.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five steps of the selection process.
questions.solution_md: Any five steps in order, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Preliminary screening:** application forms are checked and **unqualified** applicants are eliminated.
2. **Selection tests:** intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade and interest tests measure **ability and potential**.
3. **Employment interview:** an **in-depth conversation** judges suitability and exchanges information.
4. **Reference and background checks:** former employers and referees are contacted to verify **character and record**.
5. **Selection decision:** the final choice is made from those who passed the earlier steps, usually by the **manager** concerned.

questions.stem_md: Prakash Engineering (imagined) is hiring trainee machine operators, sales executives and a quality inspector. Explain five selection tests and suggest which job each would suit best.
questions.solution_md: Five tests explained, each linked to the job it best suits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Intelligence test:** measures general mental ability (IQ); useful for **all** posts, especially where decisions are needed.
2. **Aptitude test:** measures **potential to learn**; suits **trainee operators**, who will be trained on machines.
3. **Personality test:** probes emotions, maturity and values; suits **sales executives**, who deal with customers.
4. **Trade test:** measures **existing skill**; suits the **quality inspector**, who must already know inspection methods.
5. **Interest test:** finds likes and dislikes about work; helps place each person in a job they will **enjoy and stay in**.

questions.stem_md: Training is best described as

options.text_md: the overall growth of an individual in all respects
increasing general knowledge and understanding of the total environment
a process of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job
choosing the best candidate for a vacancy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a process of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job. Training is job-specific. Overall growth is development; general knowledge and understanding is education; choosing candidates is selection.

questions.stem_md: New operators at an imagined bottling plant in Nagpur practise on a copy of the filling machine set up in a separate hall, so that mistakes do not stop the real production line. This method is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** vestibule training. Training on equipment similar to the real one, in a separate place away from the work floor, is vestibule training. It is used for costly or complex machines.

questions.stem_md: Salim joins an imagined electrical contractor in Lucknow and works under a master electrician for two years, learning wiring and repairs on real jobs. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an apprenticeship programme. Learning a skilled trade over a long period under the guidance of a master worker is an apprenticeship programme, an on-the-job method.

questions.stem_md: Management trainees at Narmada Fabrics (imagined) spend three months each in purchase, production, sales and accounts before getting a permanent posting. This method is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** job rotation. Moving trainees from one department to another to give them broad experience is job rotation, an on-the-job method.

questions.stem_md: Under an agreement between an imagined polytechnic in Pune and a car-parts maker, students study theory in college and work in the factory for one semester. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** internship training. A joint programme of an educational institution and a business, combining classroom theory with practical work, is internship training.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an **off-the-job** training method?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Programmed instruction. Programmed instruction (learning from material broken into small units in a logical order) is off the job. Coaching, apprenticeship and job rotation happen while doing the job.

questions.stem_md: Which is a benefit of training to the **employee** rather than to the organisation?

options.text_md: Less wastage of materials and lower costs for the firm
Better career opportunities and higher earnings from improved skills
A ready supply of future managers for the firm
Lower labour turnover in the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Better career opportunities and higher earnings from improved skills. Improved skills open better careers and higher pay for the employee. Lower wastage, a supply of future managers and lower turnover benefit the organisation.

questions.stem_md: Coaching, internship and job rotation are ___-the-job methods of training, while films and case studies are ___-the-job methods.
questions.solution_md: Coaching, internship and job rotation are on-the-job methods; films and case studies are off-the-job methods.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Development is a wider concept than training, because it aims at the overall growth of the individual and not only at skill for the present job.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Training builds job-related skills; development aims at the overall growth of the person and prepares them for future roles.

questions.stem_md:

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the separate practice area protects expensive machines and the production line while trainees learn.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Training reduces absenteeism and labour turnover in an organisation.

**Reason (R):** Training is a waste of money because trained employees always leave the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: trained, confident employees are more satisfied and stay. R is false: training is an investment that raises productivity; it does not make employees always leave.

questions.stem_md: Match each training method used by an imagined hospital chain with its description.

Staff practise on a software simulation of a busy emergency ward
A senior nurse guides a new nurse on the ward and checks her work

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Guidance by a superior on the job is coaching; a software simulation is computer modelling; analysing a real-life account is a case study; an expert talking to a group is a classroom lecture.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between training and development on any two bases.
questions.solution_md: Two bases, both sides stated for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** training increases **skills for a particular job**; development aims at the **overall growth** of the individual.
2. **Focus:** training is **job-oriented** and for the present; development is **career-oriented** and prepares people for future roles.

questions.stem_md: How do on-the-job training methods differ from off-the-job methods? Give one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Contrast the place and manner of learning and give a correct example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **On-the-job** methods train employees **while they do the actual job** at the workplace, e.g. **coaching**. **Off-the-job** methods train them **away from the work floor**, in a separate place, e.g. **vestibule training** or classroom lectures.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three benefits of training to an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits to the organisation, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Less wastage:** systematic learning is better than trial and error, so **time, money and materials** are saved.
